body.text: In brief
• Gaza's reconstruction has yet to begin, its prospects tied to a disarmament deadlock and Israel's upcoming vote.
• Updated Google Maps imagery and satellite analysis show swathes of the enclave razed, with demolitions ongoing.

Three years after the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel and the ensuing Gaza war, much of the enclave still lies in ruins, and whether it is ever rebuilt may be decided by the result of Israel's upcoming election.
Many Jewish communities around the world will mark the anniversary, with commemoration services to be held in several cities in Australia.
In Israel, the handling of the October 7 attack and the three years of war afterwards have also become an election issue.

Israelis vote on 27 October in a contest widely seen as a referendum on the track record of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose government will not allow reconstruction to begin until Hamas disarms, a demand the group refuses to meet until Israeli troops withdraw.

Nearly a year into a tenuous ceasefire, the United Nations says almost all of Gaza's 2.1 million people have been displaced, most of them living in tents and makeshift shelters across hundreds of overcrowded sites.
Updated satellite imagery on Google Maps shows entire neighbourhoods in Rafah, Khan Younis and Gaza City reduced to rubble or cleared to bare earth.
Martin Kear, a lecturer in international relations at the University of Sydney, said the stalemate that has left Gaza's reconstruction on hold is no accident.
"I would say it's in indefinite limbo and that was the way that Israel intended it to be," he told SBS News.
"Nothing happens in Gaza without the Israeli government's say-so."

In August, Netanyahu rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan that outlined the steps for Hamas disarmament and Israeli withdrawal from Gaza. Hamas had agreed to the plan in an extraordinary concession, but Netanyahu rejected the plan over concerns Hamas could immediately re-arm outside Gaza, and that deradicalisation was no longer mentioned as part of the plan.
"The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed," he said at the time.
Living among the ruins

On 7 October 2023, Hamas-led militants breached the heavily fortified barrier separating Gaza from Israel, some flying over it with paragliders, and attacked army posts, civilian towns and a music festival in southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostage.

The attack was primarily led by the Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades — also known as the Qassam Brigades — the military arm of Hamas. At least five other Palestinian armed groups are also believed to have been involved.
Israel's ensuing bombardment of Gaza has devastated much of the besieged enclave, destroying or damaging the homes of more than 60 per cent of its population.

Gaza's health ministry has recorded more than 74,243 Palestinians killed and a further 175,232 injured since the war began. Of those injured, thousands have been maimed, with more than 6,000 people undergoing amputations.

Satellite analysis by researchers at Oregon State University estimates that 245,981 buildings have likely been damaged or destroyed since the war began. That's 74.5 per cent of all buildings that stood in Gaza before October 2023.

The researchers, who analysed satellite radar imagery of the Strip every 12 days until August this year, detected damage to more than 38,000 buildings in the first 12 days of the war alone, including nearly a third of all buildings in North Gaza.
Their data traces the destruction moving south through the enclave as the war went on, with many areas struck more than once.
The ceasefire, which took effect on 10 October last year, has not substantially halted it.

Under the truce, Israeli forces pulled back to the so-called "yellow line", a boundary marked with yellow concrete blocks that initially left about 53 per cent of Gaza under Israeli control, a share Netanyahu said in May had grown to 60 per cent.

Since October last year, the researchers have detected 25,801 likely damaged or destroyed buildings on the Israeli-held side of that line, more than three times the 7,643 recorded on the Palestinian side.

The researchers attribute much of this to Israeli demolitions, though they note that satellites can detect change but not its cause, and that some of it may reflect rubble being cleared or tents being moved.
Rebuilding, meanwhile, has barely begun, with Israel barring the entry of almost all construction materials. Israel cites security concerns over the potential use of such materials by Hamas.
The UN estimates the war has left about 61 million tonnes of rubble, beneath which more than 8,000 Palestinians are still missing.
Not one hospital in the enclave is fully functional, and medical supplies wait a median of 74 days for Israeli approval to enter, according to the World Health Organization.

"Problems with water, sanitation, shelter and waste management persist, while reliance on aid and cash assistance remains high," the UN's humanitarian coordinator for the occupied Palestinian territory, Ramiz Alakbarov, said last week.
"Gazans are tired, they want back to normal life, they are asking to not live another winter in tents."
Who pays, and who governs
A joint assessment by the UN, the European Union and the World Bank in April put the cost of rebuilding Gaza at $US71.4 billion ($101.9 billion) over a decade.

United States President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, which oversees the ceasefire plan, has drawn about $US17 billion ($24.4 billion) in pledges, and last month unveiled a $US2.45 billion ($3.5 billion) first-phase blueprint it conceded it had not fully funded.

"I don't think anyone has any genuine faith in what happens after the Israeli election, what happens after 2028," Kear said, referring to the next US presidential election, when Donald Trump's term ends.
Endorsed by the UN Security Council in November, the board is chaired by Trump, and its executive includes Jared Kushner and former British prime minister Tony Blair, but no Palestinians.

Beneath it sits the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, a panel of Palestinian technocrats vetted by Israel, confined to civil affairs and, nine months after its formation, still based in Cairo.
The Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the occupied West Bank, has been sidelined.
UN human rights experts condemned the arrangement in March, warning that "the right of Palestinians to self-determination is inalienable, it is not a conditional privilege".

Kear described as "farcical" a US and Israeli proposal to rebuild only in areas under Israeli control or the committee's authority, leaving Palestinians to choose between the occupation and "whatever remains of Gaza that is uninhabitable".
What the election could change
Netanyahu told his cabinet in July: "There will be no reconstruction in Gaza without dismantling and demilitarising the Strip."
Polls suggest Netanyahu's bloc remains short of a majority, with former prime minister Naftali Bennett and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot his main challengers.
Bennett's Gaza policy states Hamas must be dismantled and disarmed and this requires diplomatic as well as military measures.
Eisenkot has said Israel can't accept an arrangement where Hamas survives.

Kear doubts the result will matter for Gaza: "If there's a new government that gets sworn in, whether that includes Netanyahu or not, I don't think it'll change anything with respect to reconstruction."
He suggested that under a returned Netanyahu government, Israeli forces may annex part of the West Bank.

Under the Oslo Accords of the 1990s, the West Bank was divided into three zones, with Area C, about 60 per cent of the territory, left under full Israeli civil and security control, pending a final peace deal that was never reached.
In February, the government moved to make it easier for Jews to buy property in the West Bank, which right-wing ministers hailed as aiding the development of Jewish communities.
Kear warns that the futures of both Gaza and the West Bank are bound together.
"In which case, there is no Palestinian state, and if there's no Palestinian state, there's no Palestinians as a separate national group, and this is what is at stake now."
